Complainant:
Mr Nick Johnson t/a Nick065

Respondent:

2. The Domain Names:
caravandelivery.co.uk
staticcaravandelivery.co.uk
3. Procedural History:
3.1 The Expert has confirmed that he is independent of each of the parties and
that, to the best of his knowledge and belief, there are no facts or
circumstances, past or present, or that could arise in the foreseeable future,
that need be disclosed as they might be of such a nature as to call in to
question his independence in the eyes of one or both of the Parties.
1

3.2 Timeline
24 March 2026 16:39 Dispute received
25 March 2026 14:26 Complaint validated
25 March 2026 14:41 Notification of complaint sent to parties
15 April 2026 02:30 Response reminder sent
16 April 2026 16:07 Response received
16 April 2026 16:07 Notification of response sent to parties
21 April 2026 09:12 Reply received
21 April 2026 09:12 Notification of reply sent to parties
21 April 2026 16:02 Mediator appointed
27 April 2026 09:34 Mediation started
07 May 2026 15:07 Mediation failed
07 May 2026 15:07 Close of mediation documents sent
11 May 2026 12:13 Expert decision payment received
4. Factual Background
4.1 This is a case where, despite each of the Parties submitting evidence in
support of their submissions, there is next to no evidence before the Expert
about the Complainant, the Respondent, their respective businesses or the
relationship between them, other than that the Parties appear to be related
and there appears to have been some dealings between them regarding
control, responsibility for payments, and use in respect of at least one of the
Domain Names (on which, further detail is set out in section 6 below).
4.2 The Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk> was registered on 25 August
2022, and the Domain Name <staticcaravandelivery.co.uk> was registered on
18 December 2024.
4.3 The Complainant paid for the first renewal of the Domain Name
<caravandelivery.co.uk> on 24 August 2023 through a company called Web
Placements Ltd acting as a registrar.
4.4 On 12 April 2024, the Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk> was transferred
from registrar Web Placements Ltd to a third party registrar under the
business known as Flagship Media Group Ltd. This Domain Name was
renewed by the Respondent in August 2024, acting through Flagship Media
Group Ltd.
5. Parties’ Contentions
5.1 The following is a brief summary of the contentions of the parties as set out
in their respective submissions.
Complaint
2

5.2 The Complainant claims that they are the rightful beneficial owner of the
Domain Names.
5.3 The Complainant submits that:
5.3.1 the Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk> was originally acquired on
their behalf through Web Placements Ltd. Payment for this Domain
Name and associated services was made by the Complainant, and this
Domain Name was used as part of the Complainant’s established
vehicle logistics business; and
5.3.2 the Domain Name <staticcaravandelivery.co.uk> was also registered
on their behalf, through a company called Flagship Web Design Ltd.
5.4 The Complainant asserts that they have consistently acted as the party
responsible for the Domain Names, including making payments, managing
associated business use, and maintaining the commercial identity attached to
them, and accordingly they have full rights and entitlement to the Domain
Names.
5.5 The Complainant says that at no point did they authorise any transfer,
reassignment, or change of control of the Domain Names to any third party,
and that any such change has occurred without their knowledge or consent.
The Complainant claims that the Domain Names have been placed under the
Respondent’s control without authorisation and as such, the Respondent has
no legitimate claim to ownership of the Domain Names.
5.6 The Complainant submits that the Respondent has made payments to the
Complainant during the period in which the Respondent was permitted to
use the Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk>. The Complainant says that
these payments were made on a recurring basis and reflect a commission
arrangement for use of the Domain Name, not ownership of it, which
establishes that the Respondent’s use of this Domain Name was conditional
and authorised by the Complainant, and that the Respondent recognised the
Complainant’s control and entitlement to it.
5.7 Further, the Complainant notes that correspondence from Flagship Web
Design Ltd contains inconsistencies, including references to alleged “proof”
from the Respondent, which has never been produced. This raises serious
concerns regarding the handling of the Domain Names and the basis upon
which control has been attributed to the Respondent.
5.8 The Complainant contends that the Respondent’s actions have disrupted
their business, interfered with their ability to operate under established
trading names, and prevented them from using domain names that were
acquired specifically for their commercial activities.
3

Response
5.9 The Respondent says that:
5.9.1 Flagship Media Group Ltd has authorised the Respondent to act and
speak on their behalf in relation to the Domain Names; and
5.9.2 the Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk> was transferred into the
registrar account of Flagship Media Group Ltd in April 2024, and from
that point onwards this Domain Name was under Flagship’s registrar
control and any access to it was governed by Flagship’s internal
account structure.
5.10 The Respondent submits that on 9 May 2024 Flagship issued the Respondent
with an invoice for (i) renewal of the Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk>
for the forthcoming year and (ii) website package services in respect of this
Domain Name, which the Respondent says they paid in full. The Respondent
asserts that no evidence has been provided showing that the Complainant
paid for any domain renewals or services after this Domain Name moved to
Flagship in April 2024. The Respondent says that all renewal and service
payments during 2024–2025 were made by them, and the Domain Name was
hosted, updated, and maintained for them throughout (which the
Respondent says is still the case, always has been, and at no point did the
Complainant request access or object to the renewal at the time it occurred).
5.11 The Respondent says that the Complainant has presented no evidence of (i)
the Complainant paying for this Domain Name in 2024–2025, (ii) the
Complainant maintaining this Domain Name, (iii) active business use in that
period, or (iv) technical control or DNS access. In addition, the Respondent
asserts that the Complainant has not demonstrated Rights under the DRS
Policy and that the Complainant’s assertions relate to historic events, not
current registrant rights.
5.12 The Respondent claims that voice recordings in their possession show that (i)
the Respondent is the active owner of the Domain Names and pays for the
renewal, (ii) the Complainant authorised the transfer of the Domain Name
<caravandelivery.co.uk> to the Respondent, and (iii) the Respondent is the
owner of the Domain Name and runs it.
5.13 The Respondent submits that (i) they have issued invoices to customers
under the Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk> which include the
Respondent’s details as the owner of the website and business, and (ii) the
managing director of Flagship has confirmed that they agree that the
Respondent owns the Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk>.
Reply
4

5.14 The Complainant repeats their claims that (i) they acquired and paid for the
Domain Names, (ii) at no point was ownership of either Domain Name
formally transferred or sold to the Respondent, (iii) any use of the Domain
Names by the Respondent was with the Complainant’s permission only.
5.15 The Complainant says that any business activity carried out by the
Respondent using the Domain Names arose with the Complainant’s
knowledge, permission, and ongoing support. This included guidance on
website structure, operational approach, and general business setup. The
Respondent’s use of the Domain Names was therefore not independent, but
formed part of a broader arrangement in which the Complainant allowed
their use to assist the Respondent.
5.16 The registrar changes referenced by the Respondent are, says the
Complainant, administrative changes only and do not constitute a transfer of
ownership.
5.17 The Complainant says that when the Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk>
was moved from its original provider to Flagship, the Complainant
understood that they remained the registrant, having originally purchased
and paid for the Domain Name and that the Complainant had no reason to
believe otherwise and was not made aware of any change to the registrant
position at that time. It only became apparent during this dispute that the
registrant details did not reflect the Complainant’s ownership. The
Complainant says that this demonstrates that administrative records and
registrar arrangements have not consistently aligned with the underlying
ownership position and should not be relied upon as determinative of
ownership.
5.18 The Complainant says that this is further illustrated by the handling of the
Domain Name <staticcaravandelivery.co.uk>, where the Domain Name was
purchased on the Complainant’s instruction and payment was made by the
Complainant, but despite this control was later attributed to the Respondent.
5.19 The Complainant says that there is no signed agreement, invoice, or formal
documentation evidencing that ownership of either Domain Name was ever
transferred from the Complainant to the Respondent.
5.20 The Complainant submits that they formally requested that one of the
Domain Names (unspecified) be returned to them in September 2025, and
that at the time of this request the Complainant had been paying the ongoing
charges associated with the Domain Name, having previously taken over
those payments to ensure continuity when the Respondent failed to do so.
Following the Complainant’s request in September 2025 for the Domain
Name to be returned, the billing arrangements were changed and charges
were subsequently directed to the Respondent instead. The Complainant
5

says that this change in billing was made without their authority or
instruction, and without any notification to them at the time.
5.21 The Complainant further submits that the Respondent had previously made
regular payments to the Complainant in connection with the Respondent’s
use of the Domain Name (again, unspecified). These payments were made as
part of the arrangement under which the Respondent was permitted to use
the Domain Name, rather than as owner. When those payments ceased, the
Complainant withdrew permission for the Respondent to continue using the
Domain Name and formally requested that control be returned to the
Complainant.
5.22 The Complainant contends that the present situation appears to stem from
administrative arrangements made by the provider at the time, rather than
any transfer of ownership or intention to relinquish the Complainant’s rights.
6. Discussions and Findings
6.1 For the Complainant to succeed with their Complaint, they are required
under paragraphs 2.1 and 2.2 of the Nominet Dispute Resolution Policy (the
“Policy”) to prove to the Expert, on the balance of probabilities, that:
(1) the Complainant has Rights in respect of a name or mark which is
identical or similar to the Domain Name; and
(2) the Domain Name, in the hands of the Respondent, is an Abusive
Registration.
Rights
6.2 Paragraph 1 of the Policy provides that Rights means “rights enforceable by
the Complainant, whether under English law or otherwise, and may include
rights in descriptive terms which have acquired a secondary meaning”. Rights
may be established in a name or mark by way of a trade mark registered in an
appropriate territory, or by a demonstration of unregistered rights, such as
rights acquired through use of a name.
6.3 Further guidance on what is required for a Complainant to prove that
he/she/it “has rights” in paragraph 2.1.1 of the Policy is set out in section 2.2
of the ‘Dispute Resolution Service - Experts’ Overview’, a document published
by Nominet on its website to assist all participants or would-be participants in
disputes under the Policy by explaining commonly raised issues and how
Experts, the members of Nominet’s panel of independent adjudicators, have
dealt with those issues to date. This section of the Experts’ Overview states
as follows:
6

“As indicated above, the relevant right has to be an enforceable right
(i.e. a legally enforceable right). Bare assertions will rarely suffice. The
Expert needs to be persuaded on the balance of probabilities that
relevant rights exist. The Expert will not expect the same volume of
evidence as might be required by a court to establish goodwill or
reputation, but the less straightforward the claim, the more evidence
the better (within reason – this is not an invitation to throw in the
‘kitchen sink’).
If the right arises out of a trade mark or service mark registration, a
copy of the registration certificate or print out from the registry
database will suffice together with, in the case of a licensee, evidence
of the licence. If the Complainant can demonstrate that it is a
subsidiary or associated company of the registered proprietor, the
relevant licence, if asserted, will ordinarily be assumed. [Appeal
decision in DRS 00248 (seiko-shop.co.uk)].
If the right is an unregistered trade mark right, evidence needs to be
put before the Expert to demonstrate the existence of the right. This
will ordinarily include evidence to show that (a) the Complainant has
used the name or mark in question for a not insignificant period and to
a not insignificant degree (e.g. by way of sales figures, company
accounts etc) and (b) the name or mark in question is recognised by
the purchasing trade/public as indicating the goods or services of the
Complainant (e.g. by way of advertisements and advertising and
promotional expenditure,
correspondence/orders/invoices from third parties and third party
editorial matter such as press cuttings and search engine results).
If the right is a contractual right, the Expert will need to see evidence
of the contract.”
6.4 The Complainant claims that they are the rightful beneficial owner of the
Domain Names, and that at some point following the Complainant’s
registration of them, the Domain Names have been placed under the
Respondent’s control without authorisation.
6.5 In support of their claim regarding ownership, the Complainant has provided
by way of evidence a copy of an invoice dated 18/12/2024 and issued by
Flagship Web Design Ltd to “MR NICK JOHNSTONE T/A NICK065”. This invoice
refers to “Domain name registration (annual fee)(staticcaravandelivery.co.uk)
(Qty1)” and is in the amount of £33.60 including VAT. This appears to support
the Complainant’s claim that they were the initial registrant of the
<staticcaravandelivery.co.uk> Domain Name (assuming that the reference to
the surname of the recipient of the invoice contained a typo, and given that
the invoice date matches the registration date of this Domain Name).
7

6.6 The relevant evidence provided by the Complainant in an attempt to support
their claim that they were the initial registrant of the <caravandelivery.co.uk>
Domain Name comprises in summary:
6.6.1 an invoice dated 03/07/2024 and issued by Web Placements Ltd to
“Nick065” which refers to “Domain Renewel [sic] Domain
Renewals/SSL’s” and sets out a list of domain names, including the
Domain Name <caravandelivery.co.uk> (which invoice follows what
appears to be email correspondence between the Complainant and a
representative of Web Placements Ltd);
6.6.2 a screenshot of (what the Complainant purports to be) an undated
email from someone called “Keanon” (who describes themselves as a
“Former webplacements employee”) in which they say, inter alia, that
in 2022 they secured the <caravandelivery.co.uk> Domain Name for
“Nick Johnson of nick065” and that they can also confirm that this
Domain Name was “purchased at the end of August 2022 and Nick
was invoiced for it on or abouts the 12th Sep 2022” (the “Keanon
Email”);
6.6.3 an email exchange from January 2026 between the Complainant and
a person named ‘Derek Carstairs’ who appears to be involved with
Flagship in which, inter alia, (1) there is an indirect reference to the
Parties possibly being related to each other; (2) the Complainant
queries the transfer of the <caravandelivery.co.uk> Domain Name
away from them; (3) the Complainant claims that while the
Respondent may have had their agreement to use this Domain Name
at the time, there was no agreement or authorisation for billing
responsibility, hosting control, or payment details to be transferred
away from the Complainant; and (4) the Complainant mentions that
(i) they made it clear to the Respondent that it was the Respondent’s
responsibility to cover the ongoing monthly hosting costs for the
<caravandelivery.co.uk> Domain Name, (ii) while the Respondent
made the initial payments, one of his payments subsequently failed at
which point Flagship contacted the Complainant directly to advise
that the payment had not gone through, (iii) to avoid any risk of the
hosting being suspended or the Domain Name being affected, the
Complainant instructed Flagship to bill them instead, and (iv) from
that point onward the Complainant made the monthly payments
consistently and without interruption until September; and
6.6.4 a screenshot of an email dated 23 September 2025 purporting to be
from ‘Paul Alker’ of Flagship Web Design which states, inter alia, “The
website is owned by Harry as he paid for it, The domain
https://www.caravandelivery.co.uk/is owned and bought by Nick”.
8

6.7 It is important to note that in respect of the invoice referred to in paragraph
6.6.1 above, the Complainant has also provided a screenshot of what appears
to be correspondence from ‘Derek Carstairs’ to Nominet dated 5/12/2025
headed “Response” in which the sender refers, inter alia, to the Respondent
maintaining that this invoice was issued in error and that Webplacements
submitted a new invoice with the <caravandelivery.co.uk> Domain Name
removed. The Expert also notes that there is reference to cancellation of this
invoice in a copy of an email submitted by the Respondent in their evidence
bundle which appears to be sent from a representative of Webplacements to
the Respondent and is dated 13 April 2026 (the “Webplacements Email”).
6.8 In addition, the Webplacements Email includes statements regarding the
legitimacy of the Keanon Email and demands that the Keanon Email should
be withdrawn as evidence also given that the purported sender of that email
had no authority to discuss any client matters after their employment ended.
6.9 In light of the above, while the Complainant may have a claim to being the
initial registrant of at least the <staticcaravandelivery.co.uk> Domain Name,
there is a significant amount of conflicting evidence provided in each party’s
submissions dealing with ownership and entitlement, and there are doubts
regarding the veracity of each party’s submissions and evidence. In that
respect, it is important for the Parties to note that the DRS is designed to be a
simple, efficient and low cost system for resolving domain name disputes. It
is not a procedure which allows the Expert to cross-examine the parties or
further test the veracity of the submissions and evidence put before them.
6.10 In any event, the Expert considers that rights to deal with the registration of a
domain name do not of themselves constitute Rights for the purposes of the
Policy, as they are not rights in respect of the name or mark itself. Further,
whether or not the Complainant was the original registrant of either or both
of the Domain Names, it appears that there has been some kind of pre-
existing relationship between the Parties regarding the use of the Domain
Names subsequent to their registration.
6.11 Turning now to the question of whether the Complainant has registered
and/or unregistered rights such that it can make out their case on Rights
pursuant to and in accordance with the Policy, the Complainant has not
asserted that they own or have a licence to use any registered trade or
service marks that they could rely on to make out their case in respect of
Rights, nor is there any evidence before the Expert of this being the case.
6.12 Further, while the Complainant’s submissions makes reference to their
business and their operations conducted under established trading names,
these are bare assertions and the Complainant has given no explanation nor
provided any evidence of what this business and operations are, how long
they have been in existence for, and whether the “established trading
9

names” are names that correspond or relate to either or both of the Domain
Names.
6.13 In addition, none of the material mentioned in section 2.2 of the Experts’
Overview (as set out above) for a Complainant to demonstrate existence of
an unregistered trade mark has been provided by the Complainant. The
Complainant has not provided any evidence of usage, sales figures, company
accounts, advertising/marketing activities or expenditure, correspondence or
any of the other examples provided in such section. The Complainant has also
not provided any evidence of their use of either Domain Name at any time
subsequent to their respective registration dates, despite their claim that
they have conducted operations under established trading names.
6.14 The Complainant claims that the Respondent’s actions have interfered with
the Complainant’s ability to operate under established trading names, and
have prevented them from using domains that were acquired specifically for
their commercial activities. Again, these claims (relating to the Complainant’s
business and their commercial activities) are unsupported by any evidence.
6.15 All the Expert has before them in respect of the Complainant’s case on Rights
are bare assertions made by the Complainant, and as noted in section 2.2 of
the Experts’ Overview “Bare assertions will rarely suffice.” The Complainant
has therefore failed to demonstrate that they have any unregistered trade
mark rights in respect of a name or mark which is identical or similar to either
or both of the Domain Names.
6.16 The Complainant may well feel aggrieved if control of the Domain Names has
unintentionally or nefariously been transferred to the Respondent, but even
if that were the case (and the Expert makes no finding in that respect) on its
own that would not be sufficient for the Complainant to have proved to the
Expert, on the balance of probabilities, that they have Rights in respect of a
name or mark which is identical or similar to the Domain Names.

could arise in the foreseeable future, that need be disclosed as they might be of a

24 April 2026 10:31 Dispute received

20 May 2026 14:42 Expert decision payment received
4. Factual Background
The Complainant is a company registered in the UK since January 2017. One of the
directors of the Complainant is the owner of UK trade mark number UK00003392335
for a stylised version of the expression “Immersive Experiences” shown below (the
“Trade Mark”). The Trade Mark has a filing date of 15 April 2019 and a registration
date of 16 August 2019.
The Trade Mark is registered in respect of a wide range of goods and services,
including “provision of exhibitions for entertainment purposes” and “entertainment
services”.
The Complainant has provided a broad description of its trading activities in relation
to the provision of immersive dome experiences, mobile planetariums, and
educational workshops across the UK. However, no evidence of its trading activity
(such as advertising, social media following, invoices, company accounts, turnover
data, third party media coverage, public reviews, etc.) has been provided, save for a
link to its website at <immersive-experiences.co.uk> where it is clear that the
Complainant trades under the name “Immersive Experiences”.
The Respondent is an individual who operates a business trading under the name
"Immersive Theatres 360° Experiences", operating from the domain name
<immersive-theatres.com>. The Respondent’s business appears to be very similar (if
not identical) to that of the Complainant, being the provision of portable inflatable
2

domes within which an audio-visual educational or entertainment “experience” is
projected for the benefit of an audience within the dome.
5. Parties’ Contentions
The Complainant asserts that, as the owner of the Trade Mark, they have exclusive
rights to use that brand and prevent any confusingly similar brands from being used
by third parties in connection with activities similar to those covered by the Trade
Mark.
The Complainant also asserts that they have developed unregistered rights
protected by the law of passing off as a result of their trading in the “immersive
experiences sector” in the last decade. Their position is that the relevant public
associate the name “Immersive Experiences” with the Complainant.
The Complainant’s position is that the Domain Name constitutes an Abusive
Registration because it targets the Complainant’s established brand, creates
confusion in the marketplace, diverts customers, and disrupts the Complainant’s
business operations. The Complainant also contends that the registration and use of
the Domain Name is an attempt to “free ride” on the Complainant’s reputation in
bad faith.
The Respondent submits that the use of the expression “Immersive Experiences” as
part of the Domain Name is descriptive since the Respondent’s business is the
provision of “immersive experiences”.
The Complainant submitted a Reply which reads as correspondence directed
towards the Respondent rather than submissions filed for consideration by the
Expert. The Reply has not been taken into account for the purposes of this decision
(although it is noted that the content of the Reply would not have affected the
outcome of this decision in any event).
6. Discussions and Findings
Under paragraph 2.2 of the Policy, the Complainant must prove, on the balance of
probabilities, each of the two elements set out in paragraphs 2.1.1 and 2.1.2 of the
Policy, namely that the Complainant has Rights in respect of a name or mark which is
identical or similar to the Domain Name; and that the Domain Name, in the hands of
the Respondent, is an Abusive Registration.
Rights
Paragraph 1 of the Policy provides that Rights means “rights enforceable by the
Complainant, whether under English law or otherwise, and may include rights in
descriptive terms which have acquired a secondary meaning”.
3

The requirement to demonstrate Rights under the Policy does not have a high
threshold. Rights may be established by way of a trade mark registration, or
unregistered rights arising from use of a name to the standard required under
common law.
The Complainant has provided details of the Trade Mark. The text of that trade mark
registration is identical with the text of the Domain Name. The goods and services
covered by the Trade Mark are the same as those provided by both the Complainant
and the Respondent.
This is sufficient to establish Rights for the purposes of the present complaint.
It is noted that the Trade Mark is registered in the name of “Zeeshaan Dinally” rather
than the Complainant. Zeeshaan Dinally is one of the directors of the Complainant
and shares the same contact address as the Complainant on the UK IPO records, and
the Expert is therefore content to find that the Complainant is an authorised user of
the Trade Mark for the purposes of this Complaint.
The Domain Name comprises the name “immersiveexperiences” and the top-level
domain suffix “.co.uk”, which may be disregarded for the purpose of comparison.
The text component of the Trade Mark is plainly identical with the text of the
Domain Name.
The Complainant has made extensive reference to the nature and extent of its
trading activity but has provided no evidence (save as referred to in the following
paragraph) beyond mere assertions, and the Expert attaches no weight to that part
of the Complaint.
The Complainant has demonstrated a level of trading activity through its registration
and use of the domain <immersive-experiences.co.uk>. It is clear that this is highly
similar to the Domain Name, differing only in the presence of a hyphen. The Expert
finds that the Complainant has at least a de minimis level of Rights associated with
the registration and use of its domain name, to which the Domain Name is highly
similar.
The Expert finds that the Complainant has Rights in respect of a name or mark which
is identical with or highly similar to the Domain Name.
Abusive Registration
Paragraph 1 of the Policy defines “Abusive Registration” as a domain name which
either:
i. was registered or otherwise acquired in a manner which, at the time when
the registration or acquisition took place, took unfair advantage of or was
unfairly detrimental to the Complainant's Rights; or
4

ii. is being or has been used in a manner which has taken unfair advantage of
or has been unfairly detrimental to the Complainant's Rights;
This general definition is supplemented by paragraph 5.1 of the Policy which
provides a non-exhaustive list of factors which may be evidence that the Domain
Name is an Abusive Registration. Paragraph 8.1 of the Policy provides a similar non-
exhaustive list of factors which may be evidence that the Domain Name is not an
Abusive Registration.
The Policy requires the Complainant to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that
the Domain Name is an Abusive Registration. The burden of proof is therefore firmly
on the Complainant.
The Complainant’s case is that the Respondent purposely registered the Domain
Name in the knowledge of the Complainant’s Rights for the purposes of unfairly
disrupting the Complainant’s business within the meaning of paragraph 5.1.1.3 of
the Policy, and to confuse people into thinking that the Domain Name is connected
with the Complainant under paragraph 5.1.2 of the Policy.
The Complainant has claimed to have a national footprint across the United
Kingdom, and established online presence and high online search visibility. In the
absence of supporting evidence, no finding is made on this basis.
The Complainant has also suggested that the registration and use of the Domain
name is leading to loss of enquiries and bookings, creating customer confusion, and
driving increased marketing costs to counteract confusion. Again, no evidence has
been provided of this.
The Respondent’s case is that the use oft the Domain Name
<immersiveexperienes.co.uk> is a legitimate description of their business of
providing “immersive experiences”. In other words, the Respondent seeks to rely on
paragraph 8.1.2 of the Policy in that the Domain Name is generic or descriptive and
the Respondent is making fair use of it, and therefore does not constitute an Abusive
Registration.
By their own admission, the Respondent trades under the name "Immersive
Theatres 360° Experiences" or just “Immersive Theatres” and operates from the
domain name <immersive-theatres.com>. The content of the site hosted at the
Domain Name appears to be nearly identical to that hosted on <immersive-
theatres.com>.
This leads to the question of why the Respondent, as the owner of a business
operating under the name “Immersive Theatres”, has chosen to register the Domain
Name <immersiveexperiences.co.uk> to create a mirror of its website.
Given the similarity of the names between the respective businesses of the
Complainant and the Respondent through the mutual adoption of the word
5

“Immersive”, it appears to be a strange choice on the part of the Respondent to
actively choose a domain name that (a) is different to its own trading name, and (b)
adopts the same name as a competitor in the market.
It is inconceivable that the Respondent would not have been aware of the
Complainant, either as a result of operating in the same sector, or from online
searches of the name “Immersive Experiences” prior to registration of the Domain
Name. In any event, the Response does not state that the Respondent was unaware
of the Complainant’s activities, and the Respondent does not appear to have
changed their activities in the light of the complaint and the surrounding
circumstances.
The only reasonable conclusion is that the Respondent purposely chose to register
and use the Domain Name for the purposes of unfairly disrupting the Complainant’s
business within the meaning of paragraph 5.1.1.3. The Respondent has their own
separate website at <immersive-theatres.com> and yet chose to replicate it under a
name already adopted by a competitor.
Given the Complainant’s existing Rights (and long-standing use of the domain name
<immersive-experiences.co.uk>), it is reasonable to infer that an average internet
user would assume that the Domain Name is somehow affiliated with, authorised by,
or otherwise connected to the Complainant, when that is not the case.
Customers attempting to locate the Complainant’s online presence may be diverted
to the Respondent, and given the mutual use of “Immersive” in the names and the
seemingly identical business offerings, there is clearly a risk that those customers
may be confused and may end up purchasing services from the Respondent instead
of from the Complainant. Paragraph 5.1.2 of the Policy does not require actual
confusion to be proven, but just that confusion be likely, and the Expert finds this to
be the case.
This is due to the strong similarity of the names adopted by each party, their highly
similar business offerings, the Complainant’s existing domain name, the fact that the
Respondent already has their own separate trading presence online, and the
absence of any credible reason for adopting the Domain Name having been provided
by the Respondent.
The Respondent’s submissions that the name “immersive experiences” is generic or
descriptive are noted, but are not considered sufficiently persuasive to displace the
clear inference that the use of the Domain Name by the Respondent presents a real
risk of confusion. This submission may have carried more weight if the Respondent
were actually to have been separately trading under the name “Immersive
Experiences”, but since that is not the case, and the Respondent operates under a
similar name, the finding of an Abusive Registration on the grounds that the
Respondent, on balance of probabilities, adopted the Domain Name to disrupt or
associate with the Complainant is maintained.
6

There appears to be a wider history of the dispute between the parties and the DRS
is not the forum for resolution of that dispute. For the avoidance of doubt for both
parties, this decision is made purely on the basis of the submissions of each party
and is limited in scope to whether the registration and use of the Domain Name
constitutes an Abusive Registration. No finding is made in relation to the validity or
enforceability of the Trade Mark, infringement of the Trade Mark, or in relation to
any claims for passing off, unfair competition, or reputational damage.
7. Decision
The Expert finds that the Complainant has proved that it has Rights in a name which
is highly similar to the Domain Name and that the Domain Name, in the hands of the
Respondent, is an Abusive Registration. The Expert therefore directs that the Domain
Name be transferred to the Complainant.
Signed Dated 26 May 2026
Simon Sellars

3. Procedural Background
On 26th March 2026, the Complaint was lodged with Nominet UK Limited (“Nominet”) and it was
validated on 27th March 2026. On 27th March 2026, Nominet sent the notification of the Complaint
letter to the Respondent by e-mail and post, advising the Respondent to log into Nominet’s online
services to view the details of the Complaint, and giving the Respondent 15 business days within
which to lodge a Response on or before 21st April 2026. On 17th April 2026, Nominet sent the
Respondent a Response reminder. On 21st April 2026, the Respondent sent a Response. On 21st April
2026, Nominet advised the Complainant that a Response had been received and advised it to log
into Nominet’s Online Services to view it. Nominet invited the Complainant to make a Reply on or
before 28th April 2026. On 24th April 2026, Nominet sent the Complainant a Reply reminder. On 28th
April 2026, the Complainant sent a Reply. On 28th April 2026, Nominet advised the Respondent a
Reply had been received. Mediation documents were generated for the Complaint, and mediation

the appropriate fee for a Decision to be made by an Expert pursuant to paragraph 6 of Nominet’s
DRS Policy (“the Policy”).
On 12th May 2026, Mr Niall Lawless (“the Expert”) was notified of his appointment to act as Expert
in this dispute and is required to give his Decision by 8th June 2026. The Expert has confirmed that
he is independent of each of the Parties and that, to the best of his knowledge and belief, there are
no facts or circumstances, past or present, or that could arise in the foreseeable future, that need
to be disclosed as they might be of such a nature as to call into question his independence in the
eyes of one or both of the Parties.
On 14th May 2026, Nominet sent the Parties an “Expert Request for Further Information”: “The
Expert notes that whereas the Complaint refers to Annex 1 to 7, the Annexes document available via
Nominet online services appears to consist only of one cover page “Annex 1”. Pursuant to paragraph
17.1 of the Policy, the Expert offers the Complainant the opportunity to submit Annex 1 to 7 before
the end of Wednesday 20th May 2026. Should the Respondent wish to make any submissions in
respect of Annex 1 to 7, it should do so before the end of Wednesday, 27th May 2026.”
On 18th May 2026, the Complainant submitted the Complaint Annex 1 to 7. The Respondent made
no submissions in respect of Annex 1 to 7.
2

4. Outstanding Formal or Procedural Issues
There are no outstanding formal or procedural issues.
5. Factual Background
The Complainant, Cash Converters Pty Limited and its subsidiary Cash Converters (UK) Limited
(individually or together "Cash Converters") was formed in 1984 and first opened its CASH
CONVERTERS branded business in the UK in 1991. It is a global retail and financial services company
that specialises in buying and selling second-hand goods and providing financial services, including
lines of credit.
The Respondent, Cash Conversions, serving the local community in Leeds, UK, since 2011, specialises
in buying gold, electronics, and other items of value, providing instant cash with no hidden fees or
hassle.
The Respondent registered the Domain Name on 7th July 2011, and it resolves to a website
promoting its products and services.
6. The Parties’ Contentions
The Complainant
The Complainant says that it has rights in a name that is identical to the Domain Name, and it seeks
transfer of the Domain Name.
In summary, the Complainant says that the Domain Name in the hands of the Respondent is abusive
because:
• The Domain Name is being used in a way is likely to confuse people or businesses into believing
that the Domain Name is registered to, operated or authorised by, or otherwise connected with
the Complainant.
• The Domain Name resolves to a website where the content offered is identical and/or similar
services to that of the Complainant.
• The Domain Name resolves to a website that shares a colour scheme and format with that of the
Complainant.
• Any misrepresentation of an affiliation or association with the Complainant is likely to disrupt its
business by way of consumer confusion, which may tarnish the reputation of the Complainant
and/or result in a loss of sales.
3

• The Respondent’s use of the Domain Name takes “unfair advantage” because the Respondent
has benefitted from the Complainant’s repute without expending any effort of its own.
• The Respondent has not provided any evidence to support its position.
• There is no connection or co-operation between the Complainant and the Respondent.
The Respondent
In summary, the Respondent says that the Domain Name is not an Abusive Registration because:
• It has traded under the name “Cash Conversions” for a long period of time.
• It is an independent business and has never claimed to be the Complainant.
• It has not created a misleading imitation website.
• The Domain Name matches its genuine trading name.
• The Domain Name was registered for legitimate business use.
• The Domain Name has been used in connection with genuine business activity.
• The Domain Name was not registered for sale, disruption, deception, or unfair gain.
• There has been no unfair advantage taken of the Complainant’s rights.
• There has been no unfair detriment caused to the Complainant.
• The Complaint does not establish abusive registration as required by the Policy.
7. Discussion and Findings
7.1 General
The Policy requires that for a Complaint to succeed, the Complainant must prove to the Expert on the
balance of probabilities that:
i. the Complainant has Rights in respect of a name or mark which is identical or similar to the
Domain Name; and
ii. the Domain Name, in the hands of the Respondent, is an Abusive Registration.
Rights include, but are not limited to, rights enforceable under English law.
7.2 The Complainant’s Rights
The Complainant’s name is Cash Converters Pty Limited, and its UK subsidiary is Cash Converters (UK)
Limited. The Complainant has provided evidence that it is the proprietor of a number of registered
trademarks for CASH CONVERTERS including UK Trademark numbers UK00001463232 registered on
1st October 1993 and UK00002588064 registered on 25th November 2011; and European Union
4

trademark number 001810498 registered on 10th October 2003 and the comparable United Kingdom
trademark No. UK00901810498 created following the United Kingdom’s exit from the European
Union, and also treated as registered on 10th October 2003; In the UK the Complainant conducts
business at <www.cashconverters.co.uk>.
The Domain Name is similar to the Complainant’s name and the ‘CASH CONVERTERS” trademark and
the Complainant’s UK trading domain name.
Accordingly, based on the evaluation of the evidence presented, the Expert decides that the
Complainant has Rights in respect of a name or mark that is identical or similar to the Domain Name.
7.3 Abusive Registration
The Complainant says that the Domain Name controlled by the Respondent is an Abusive Registration
under the Policy. Under paragraph 5 “Evidence of Abusive Registration”, guidance is given as to what
factors may be evidence that the Domain Name is an Abusive Registration.
“A non-exhaustive list of factors which may be evidence that the Domain Name is an Abusive
Registration is as follows:
5.1.1 Circumstances indicating that the Respondent has registered or otherwise acquired the Domain
Name primarily:
5.1.1.1 for the purposes of selling, renting or otherwise transferring the Domain Name to the
Complainant or to a competitor of the Complainant, for valuable consideration in excess of the
Respondent's documented out-of-pocket costs directly associated with acquiring or using the
Domain Name;
5.1.1.2 as a blocking registration against a name or mark in which the Complainant has Rights; or
5.1.1.3 for the purpose of unfairly disrupting the business of the Complainant;
5.1.2 Circumstances indicating that the Respondent is using or threatening to use the Domain Name
in a way which has confused or is likely to confuse people or businesses into believing that the Domain
Name is registered to, operated or authorised by, or otherwise connected with the Complainant.”
5

Confusion and unfair advantage
The Complainant
As set out above, the Complainant says that the Domain Name is being used in a way is likely to
confuse people or businesses into believing that the Domain Name is registered to, operated or
authorised by, or otherwise connected with the Complainant.
To support this contention, the Complainant says that the Domain Name resolves to a website where
the content is identical and/or similar services to that of the Complainant, and that the website shares
the same colour scheme and format as that of the Complainant.
The Complainant says that, on the balance of probabilities, the Respondent has, from the time it
registered the Domain Name on 7th July 2011, taken unfair advantage benefitting from the repute of
the Complainant’s Cash Converters marks without expending any effort of its own. The Complainant
supports this contention by referring the Expert to Cash Converters Pty Limited and Cash Converters
(UK) Limited) Annual Report 2011, which records that the Cash Converters UK online store generated
39,043,271 page views, from 2,144,386 unique visitors.
The Respondent
The Respondent says that similarity between the names “Cash Conversions” and “Cash Converters” is
not enough to cause confusion.
The Responding Party says that its longstanding use of the name “Cash Conversions” demonstrates
that it is commonly known by that name and it has built goodwill in it through its own efforts. The
Responding Party says that over time, it has invested money, work, and reputation into promoting its
business identity. The Responding Party says the Domain Name supports that legitimate trading
presence.
Expert’s Reasoning and Decision
The Expert accepts the Complainant’s assertion that there is no connection between the Complainant
and the Respondent.
The Complainant is correct that the Respondent has not provided any evidence to support its
contentions. In the Response, the Respondent merely stated: “We reserve the right to provide further
supporting evidence if required.”
6

Confusion would arise where the internet user incorrectly assumes that the website the Domain
Names resolves to is authorised by or belongs to the Complainant.
Despite the Domain Name being registered on 7th July 2011, the Complainant has not provided any
actual evidence of confusion.
The Complainant and the Respondent are each entitled to operate in the same business space and
offer identical and/or similar services, and it is completely normal that there would be some overlap
in content and format.
However, after undertaking a review of the Complainant’s website <www.cashconverters.co.uk> and
the Respondents website <www.cashconversions.co.uk>, the Expert decides that the websites are not
similar and it is unlikely that a visitor would be confused that both websites are operated by the
Complainant.
Accordingly, the Respondents use of the Domain Name does not take “unfair advantage” of the
Complainants repute.
Under the Policy, one of the factors which may be evidence that the Domain Name is not an Abusive
Registration is that before being aware of the Complainant’s cause for complaint (not necessarily the
‘complaint’ under the DRS), the Respondent has used or made demonstrable preparations to use the
Domain Name or a domain name which is similar to the Domain Name in connection with a genuine
offering of goods or services.
The Respondent registered the Domain Name on 7th July 2011, and it resolves to a website promoting
its products and services.
The Expert notes that the “Wayback Machine” offering an Internet Archive, records the Domain Name
being used for a website as far back as 8th April 2013.
In addition to this, the website the Domain Name resolves to refers the visitor to dedicated stores
where they can have their items valued, swap foreign currency, or explore their pre-owned retail
selection. Google Maps identifies the addresses located as: “Cash Conversions Pawn shop”. The
physical premises are:
7

• Cash Conversions (Harehills): Located at 303 Harehills Lane, LS9 6AA.
• Cash Converters (Kirkgate): Located at 19 Kirkgate, LS1 6BY.
• Cash Converters (York Road): Located at 459 York Road, LS9 6TA.
• Cash Converters (Beeston): Located on Dewsbury Road.
The Expert has no hesitation in deciding that the Respondent is a legitimate business using the Domain
Name in connection with a genuine offering of goods or services.
The Respondent has offered persuasive reasons why the Domain Name is not an Abusive Registration
considering the factors as set out in paragraph 8 of the Policy.
Accordingly, the Expert concludes that under the test as set out in paragraph 5.1.2 of the Policy, in
the hands of the Respondent the Domain Name is not an Abusive Registration.
7.4 Conclusion
The Expert finds on the balance of probabilities that the Complainant has Rights in respect of a name
or mark identical or similar to the Domain Name but that the Complainant has not proved, on the
balance of probabilities, that the Domain Name in the hands of the Respondent is an Abusive
Registration.
8. Decision
For the reasons set out in detail above, the Expert directs that the Domain Name registration will
therefore remain with the Respondent.
Niall Lawless, Nominet Expert

text:

D00028773
Decision of Independent Expert
Digital Division Limited
and
Adonis Bicaj
1. The Parties:
Complainant: Digital Division Limited
Prospect Place Millennium Way
Pride Park
Derby
DE24 8HG
United Kingdom
Respondent: Adonis Bicaj
Frankfurt am Main
Germany
2. The Domain Name:
slotstemple.org.uk
3. Procedural History:
I confirm that I am independent of each of the Parties. To the best of my
knowledge and belief, there are no facts or circumstances, past or present, or that
could arise in the foreseeable future, that need be disclosed as they might be of
such a nature as to call in to question my independence in the eyes of one or both
of the Parties.
1

10 March 2026, the Dispute was received.
11 March 2026, the Complaint was validated.
11 March 2026, the Notification of Complaint was sent to the Parties.
30 March 2026, the Response reminder was sent.
02 April 2026, no Response was received.
09 April 2026, the notification of no Response was sent to the Parties.
21 April 2026, the summary/full fee reminder was sent.
22 April 2026, the Expert decision payment was received.
4. Factual Background
4.1 The Complainant was incorporated on 5 May 2015 and provides online gaming and
gambling services under the mark ‘SLOTS TEMPLE’ (the ‘Name’).
4.2 The Complainant provides such services via its website www.slotstemple.com/, which
was registered on 26 April 2012.
4.3 The Complainant holds various Internationally registered trade marks for the Name,
including in the UK UK00003609899 (as a logo), registered on 21 January 2022, and in
the EU 018560677 (as a logo), registered on 18 January 2022 (collectively, the
‘Marks’).
4.4 The Respondent registered the Domain Name on 26 June 2025.
4.5 While the Domain Name does not at the time of this Decision resolve to an active
website, the Expert has been provided by the Complainant with various screenshots of
an active website linked to the Domain Name.
5. Parties’ Contentions
5.1 For the purposes of this section of this Decision, the Expert has summarised the
submissions of the Parties but only insofar as they are relevant to the matters that the
Expert is required to determine under Nominet's Dispute Resolution Service ('DRS')
Policy (the 'Policy').
The Complaint
5.2 In summary, the Complainant submitted that the Complaint should succeed for the
reasons below.
The Complainant's Rights
- The Complainant holds Marks in the Name.
2

- The Complainant registered its .com domain name on 26 April 2012 and started
using that domain name for its website in 2015, from which it provided its
services.
- Thus, the Name has been in use by the Complainant since 2015 in connection
with online gaming and gambling websites, being over ten years of continuous
use.
- The Domain Name is an exact match to the Name and Marks, for which it has
built a reputation.
- There is no reasonable justification for any other party to use the Name and
Marks.
Abusive Registration
- The Respondent registered the Domain Name on 26 June 2025, this registration
was subsequent to the Complainant acquiring rights in the Complainant’s .com
domain name and the Name and Marks.
- The Respondent has registered or otherwise acquired the Domain Name
primarily as a blocking registration and is not making fair use of it; and, the
Respondent’s only interest in the Domain Name is to divert traffic away from the
Complainant and to use the Domain Name for phishing.
- The Respondent has chosen the Domain Name as it is identical to the Name and
Marks and the Complainant’s .com domain name. From the website associated
with the Domain Name (the ‘Website’), it is not clear that the Respondent is not
connected to the Complainant. In fact, the Complainant submitted that “[the
Respondent] strongly imply that they are.”
- The Website purports to offer goods that originate from the Complainant,
although the Complainant has not authorised the Respondent to use the Name
or Marks and the Respondent has never been an authorised seller of the
Complainant’s services.
- The Website has stated that it was owned and controlled by the Complainant,
with the wording: "Slots Temple is a modern British platform for real-money and
free-to-play slots operated by Digital Division Ltd (Company No. 09574591)."
- In addition, the Website contains links to the Complainant’s competitors’
websites. The Domain Name uses the Complainant's Name and Marks, including
the identical logo of a yellow diamond in a circle. This visual element forms part
of the Complainant's registered UK Mark.
- On the homepage of the Website, there is a linked button that states "Play Now"
referring to the gambling games that the Website purports to offer. When this
3

link is clicked, the user is redirected to another domain name which is a
gaming/gambling site that is not owned by the Complainant and which the
Complainant has no interest in.
- Therefore, consumers searching online for the Complainant are likely to enter
the Domain Name assuming that it is registered to the Complainant, using the
country code suffix .org.uk since the Complainant originated in the UK and has
built a substantial reputation in the UK. Otherwise, they will use a search engine
such as Google and are likely to come across the Domain Name.
- The Respondent may be using the Domain Name to block the Complainant
registering a domain comprising the Name and Marks in which it has rights as
set out above. The Respondent is clearly aware of the Complainant’s Name and
Marks since both feature in the Website.
- To the best of the Complainant’s knowledge and belief, the Respondent (as an
individual business, or other organisation) has not been commonly known by the
Domain Name.
The Respondent’s Response
5.3 No response was provided.
6. Discussions and Findings
General
6.1 To succeed in the Complaint, the Complainant has to prove that, pursuant to
paragraph 2 of the Policy, on the balance of probabilities:
2.1.1 [It] has Rights in respect of a name or mark which is identical or similar to
the Domain Name; and
2.1.2 The Domain Name, in the hands of the Respondent, is an Abusive
Registration.
6.2 Addressing each of these limbs in turn:
Rights in respect of a name or mark which is identical or similar to the Domain Name
6.3 The Expert considers that, for the reasons below, the requirement set out in
paragraph 2.1.1 of the Policy is met.
6.4 Paragraph 1 of the Policy defines “Rights” as:
4

[…] rights enforceable by the Complainant, whether under English law or
otherwise, and may include rights in descriptive terms which have acquired a
secondary meaning.
6.5 The Expert notes that the Complainant has registered trade marks in the Name, being
the Marks, and that the Complainant has used the Name since 2015, having built a
reputation since then in providing its online gaming services.
6.6 Noting the above, the Expert considers that, disregarding the Domain Name suffix
“.org.uk” for this purpose, the Complainant has Rights in respect of Name/Marks
identical to the Domain Name.
Abusive Registration
6.7 For the reasons set out below, the Expert considers that the Domain Name is an
Abusive Registration as defined by the Policy.
6.8 Paragraph 1 of the Policy defines "Abusive Registration" as a domain name which
either:
i. was registered or otherwise acquired in a manner which, at the time when the
registration or acquisition took place, took unfair advantage of or was unfairly
detrimental to the Complainant’s Rights; or
ii. is being or has been used in a manner which has taken unfair advantage of or
has been unfairly detrimental to the Complainant’s Rights.
6.9 In relation to the definition of Abusive Registration in sub paragraph (i), the Policy, at
paragraph 5, sets out a non-exhaustive list of factors which may be evidence that the
Domain Name is an Abusive Registration.
6.10 Specifically, the Expert considers that the factor set out at paragraph 5.1.1.3 of the
Policy (registered primarily for the purpose of unfairly disrupting the business of the
Complainant) is relevant.
6.11 Noting that the Domain Name is identical to the Complainant’s Marks, the Expert
considers that the Respondent was very aware of the Complainant, and the Name,
prior to registering the Domain Name.
6.12 Indeed, the Expert considers that the Respondent specifically chose to register the
Domain Name at that time to take advantage of the Complainant’s goodwill and
reputation, with the intention of disrupting and/or profiting from the Complainant's
business.
6.13 Therefore, for the reasons set out above, the Expert considers that the registration of
the Domain Name took unfair advantage of, and was unfairly detrimental to, the
Complainant’s Rights.
5

6.14 So far as the definition of Abusive Registration in sub paragraph (ii) is concerned, the
Expert considers that the Domain Name was and is an Abusive Registration as a result
of its manner of use by the Respondent, for the reasons explained below.
6.15 Specifically, the Expert considers that the factor set out at paragraph 5.1.2, “the
Respondent is using […] the Domain Name in a way which has confused or is likely to
confuse people or businesses into believing that the Domain Name is registered to,
operated or authorised by, or otherwise connected with the Complainant”, is relevant.
6.16 As set out in Nominet’s DRS Experts’ Overview (3rd edition, paragraph 3.3), the
‘confusion’ referred to in this factor is confusion as to the identity of the person/entity
behind the Website.
6.17 Based on the evidence provided by the Complainant, including a screenshot of the
webpages linked to the Website, which includes the Respondent’s use of the
Complainant’s brand and marketing, and that there are links to the Complainant’s
competitors’ websites, the Expert considers that the Respondent has used the Domain
Name purporting to be the Complainant.
6.18 On the balance of probabilities, the Expert considers that anyone seeing the Website
connected to the Domain Name would therefore likely be confused, at least initially,
into thinking that the Website is somehow connected with the Complainant, with the
Complainant potentially losing sales of its services and valuable reputation by such
confusion.
6.19 Furthermore, the Expert considers that the factor set out at paragraph 5.1.6 is
relevant, namely: “The Domain Name is an exact match (within the limitations of the
character set permissible in domain names) for the name or mark in which the
Complainant has Rights, the Complainant’s mark has a reputation and the Respondent
has no reasonable justification for having registered the Domain Name.”
6.20 In this regard, paragraph 6.6 above sets out that the Domain Name is identical to the
Marks, paragraph 6.5 above sets out the Expert’s view that the Complainant has a
reputation in the Marks, and in the Expert’s view the “Respondent has shown no
reasonable justification for having registered the Domain Name.”
6.21 The Expert has considered whether there is any evidence before him to demonstrate
that the Domain Name is not an Abusive Registration, including whether the
Respondent is making fair use of the Domain Name, but does not consider there is.
6.22 Therefore, for the reasons set out above, the Expert considers that the use of the
Domain Name takes unfair advantage of, and is unfairly detrimental to, the
Complainant’s Rights.
6

7. Decision
7.1 The Expert finds that, on the balance of probabilities, the Complainant has Rights in
respect of a name or mark which is identical to the Domain Name and that the
Domain Name, in the hands of the Respondent, is an Abusive Registration. Therefore,
the Expert directs that the Domain Name be transferred to the Complainant.
